items.title: 13.4 Average Translational Kinetic Energy of a Gas

source_refs.note: Topic 13.4 with the daily-life examples and For Your Information box (PDF 9-11). Fig 13.3 (a photograph of popcorn) is described. The two check questions are added; answers need review.

blocks.text: We now combine the gas law PV = nRT with the kinetic theory result PV = (1/3) N m <v^2>. Equating them: nRT = (1/3) N m <v^2> = (1/3) N m v_rms^2 (13.15), so m v_rms^2 = 3nRT/N. Since N/n = NA is the number of molecules in one mole, m v_rms^2 = 3RT/NA, which gives v_rms = square root of (3RT/(m NA)) (13.16). Using kB = R/NA, this becomes (1/2) m <v^2> = (3/2) kB T (13.17).

blocks.title: Average translational kinetic energy
blocks.text: The average translational kinetic energy of a gas molecule is <K.E.> = (1/2) m v_rms^2 = (3/2) kB T (13.18). It depends only on the absolute temperature. The pressure can also be written P = (2/3) No <K.E.>, where No is the number of molecules per unit volume.

So the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules is simply a constant times the temperature: if this model is accurate, the temperature of a gas is a direct measure of the average translational kinetic energy of its molecules. For an air molecule at room temperature (300 K), kB T = 1.38 x 10^-23 J K^-1 x 300 K = 4.14 x 10^-21 J. For such small energies the electron volt is used: 1 eV is the kinetic energy gained by an electron accelerated through a potential difference of one volt, 1 eV = 1.6 x 10^-19 J. With kB = 8.62 x 10^-5 eV K^-1, kB T at 300 K = 0.026 eV.

items: Popcorn: when a corn kernel is heated, the moisture trapped inside turns to steam. The pressure inside the kernel rises until it bursts the cover and releases the starch, which becomes solid after cooling.

Car tyres: pumping air into a tyre increases the number of air molecules in a limited volume, so there are more collisions with the tyre walls and the pressure rises. This pressure keeps the tyre firm and lets it bear the car's weight.

blocks.title: For your information
blocks.text: Kinetic theory helps us understand how pollutants interact with the atmosphere. This knowledge is used to develop systems that monitor air quality.
